extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, inventors, and law students (readers of a treatise on patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the legal criteria under English patent law for what makes an invention patentable and what sustains a patent's validity in court; focused on statutory and common‑law requirements (manner of manufacture, utility, novelty, inventiveness, authorship/origin, disclosure, and statutory limits).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent confers exclusive right in exchange for disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crown (now the Patent Office) grants an exclusive privilege (monopoly) in working an invention for a specified number of years; this privilege is secured to the inventor in exchange for 'full disclosure.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treatise frames the patent as a time‑limited monopoly: during that period the community is precluded from making use of the invention except by permission of the inventor or his successor. The monopoly exists as the quid pro quo for disclosing the invention to the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter — 'manner of manufacture'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Statute of James I (Statute of Monopolies) requires a patentable invention to be 'referable to some manner of manufacture' as interpreted by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not every discovery is patentable; courts' interpretation of 'manner of manufacture' determines whether a thing falls within patentable subject matter. The treatise restricts its scope to patents for inventions that meet this requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility (usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must possess a certain amount of utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility is stated as a precondition for a patent to be held valid in a court of law — the invention must do something useful or have a practical application (the treatise gives this as one of the core requirements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must display some degree of novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty is an essential element of validity; the treatise later connects novelty with prohibitions on deriving the invention from prior printed books or published patent specifications and with being the first inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive ingenuity (inventive step)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must have been attained by the exercise of some measure of ingenuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validity requires more than mere discovery or routine skill — there must be a demonstrable measure of ingenuity or inventive step. The treatise lists this alongside utility and novelty as the three core substantive requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: True and first inventor / origin of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The patentee must be the 'true and first inventor': he must not have obtained the invention from another person (unless imported from abroad), nor derived it from a printed book or from a patent specification published domestically or introduced from abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requirement addresses the inventor's provenance: if the claimed inventor obtained the invention from someone else or from public printed sources, that will defeat the patentee's claim to be 'true and first' and undermine validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of Monopolies limits — not contrary to law or 'mischievous to the state'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Statute of Monopolies excepts grants to the true and first inventor only so long as they are 'not contrary to law, nor mischievous to the state, by raising prices of commodities at home, or hurt of trade, or generally inconvenient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when an invention is by the first inventor, a patent will be invalid if it falls within the statute's prohibitions — e.g., if it effectively creates a harmful monopoly that injures trade or public interest. The treatise cites this statutory limitation as part of assessing validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step approach when validity is questioned
rubrics_metrics.description: When the validity of a monopoly comes into question, first consider whether it is rendered void by the statute; secondly, if not avoided by the statute, consider whether it is a privilege permitted by the common law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise prescribes a procedural/analytical order for challenges: (1) examine statutory invalidity (Statute of Monopolies) and (2) if statute does not void it, examine whether the Crown's common‑law power (and historical practice) supports the grant. This frames how courts approach disputes over patent validity.
